text: The town remembers Isaac Morrow as the man who designed the bridge. He wasn't. He was the contractor whose quarrels with the company held it up for six years, and his name is on the plaque because he paid for the plaque.
strengths: the correction arrives with the evidence for it
the plaque line is dry and earns its repeated word
weaknesses: He wasn't is the first half of a formula that machine narration leans on
the last sentence carries two facts and could be split
spokenRhythm: A medium opening for the legend, a two-word reversal, then a long sentence that settles the record and ends on a dry turn.
narrativeFunction: Introduces a man by correcting the town's memory of him.
whyItWorks: A legend the record contradicts is the one place where a flat reversal earns its place, because the listener has just been told something false and needs to hear it cancelled. The two-word line sounds like a person correcting a story at a table, and the reason his name is on the plaque gives the correction a dry payoff.
whyItFails: It wasn't X, it was Y is among the most recognisable machine patterns, and a second one anywhere nearby turns this into a tic. It also tempts the writer to stage every introduction as a debunking. Keep it once, where there is a genuine legend to correct, and use the plainer version elsewhere.
rewrite: The town remembers Isaac Morrow as the man who designed the bridge. In fact he was the contractor whose quarrels with the company held it up for six years. His name is on the plaque because he paid for the plaque.

text: By the spring, Anna Selby must have known that the mill could not pay its debts. The accounts she kept herself show it plainly. She went on buying cotton all the same, at the highest prices of the year.
strengths: the inference rests on a record she made herself
the third sentence turns the inference into tension
weaknesses: must have known states her mind as near certain
the second sentence exists to justify the first
spokenRhythm: A medium sentence of inference, a short one that cites the evidence, and a longer close that adds what she did.
narrativeFunction: Shows a mill owner carrying on in the face of her own figures, and sets up the collapse.
whyItWorks: The claim about her mind is not invented, since the next sentence names the evidence and the evidence is in her own hand. Said once, must have known sounds like a careful person reasoning aloud, and it makes her decision to keep buying all the more striking.
whyItFails: Must have is the doorway to invented interiority. Once a script allows it, the next line says she must have felt betrayed, then that she must have lain awake, and none of that is on the record. With a real person it puts a state of mind on someone who left no word of it. The safer version gives the accounts and lets the listener draw the conclusion.
rewrite: By the spring, the accounts Anna Selby kept herself showed that the mill could not pay its debts. She went on buying cotton all the same, at the highest prices of the year.

text: Why would a printer with a full order book start a newspaper that nobody in the town had asked for? Nathaniel Burke never explained it. His account books suggest he could not afford a newspaper at all.
strengths: the question is one the film cannot answer, and it says so
the evidence that follows deepens the question instead of closing it
weaknesses: opening on a question delays the man's name by a sentence
the question is long for a listener to hold
spokenRhythm: A long question, a short sentence that declines to answer it, then a medium sentence of evidence.
narrativeFunction: Introduces a printer through the puzzle of his biggest decision.
whyItWorks: The question is a real one, the kind a historian puts to the sources, and the narrator admits straight away that the man left no answer. Because the next lines add evidence rather than a reply, the question stays open and becomes the thread the next scene follows.
whyItFails: A question the narrator answers at once is a quiz, and two in a row are a habit. Openings that start with Why would also tend to reappear at the head of every section. Keep one where the record is genuinely silent, and state the puzzle plainly everywhere else.
rewrite: Nathaniel Burke had a full order book when he started a newspaper that nobody in the town had asked for. He never explained why, and his account books suggest he could not afford a newspaper at all.
